lesson.grammar_point: future perfect and future continuous for plans and timelines

listenings.text: In the academic discussion task you have about ten minutes, and I want you to divide them into three parts before you even read the question. The first minute is for the outline. Read the professor’s question and the two student posts, decide your position, and write down two reasons and one example, in single words, not sentences. The next eight minutes are for the draft. Do not repeat what the other students said; respond to one of them, and then add something new. And the last minute is sacred: you proofread. Look for the mistakes you always make, not every possible mistake. Most students skip the outline because it feels like wasted time. It is the opposite. The outline is what keeps your answer coherent when the clock starts to feel loud.

I always ask students to plan backwards. Start with the deadline and ask where you will be one week before it. By then, you will have sent your documents, and you will be waiting for an answer. Two months before that, you will have received your official score. And for that to happen, you will be taking the test about four months before the deadline, so that there is still time to retake it. Now go back further. A year before the deadline, you will be writing under real time limits every week, and by that point you will have taken at least one full practice test. When you see it like this, two years is not a long time. It is a timeline with five or six milestones, and the most important one is the first practice test, because it tells you how far you really are from the requirement.

reading.rtitle: The Essay Is Gone, the Clock Is Not
paras: For years, students preparing for the TOEFL practiced one kind of writing above all: the long essay. Since January 2026, the writing section looks very different. It has three kinds of tasks, and none of them is a traditional essay. The change sounds like good news, but it has a trap: shorter tasks leave less time to fix a bad start.

In the first task, you build sentences by putting words in the correct order, and every word has to be in the right place. In the second, you write an email for a practical situation, such as asking a professor for an extension, in about seven minutes. In the third, you join an academic discussion: you read what a professor and two students have posted, and you add your own opinion in about ten minutes.

Students who do well in the email and discussion tasks rarely write faster than others. They plan better. They spend the first minute on a quick outline: the point they want to make, two reasons and one example. They write the draft without stopping to make each sentence perfect, and they keep the last minute to proofread. A concise, coherent answer with one clear example usually does better than a long one that tries to say everything.

The same logic works for the exam date itself. A student who starts two years early does not need to study more hours. She needs a timeline with milestones, so that by the time she applies, she will have taken several practice tests and will already be writing under real time limits. The first draft of that plan is the most important piece of writing she will do.
